description: Identifying positive and negative skew, commenting on outliers, and recognising binomial and Normal distributions.
content_html:
What Is a Distribution?

When you collect a set of data, the values spread across a range. The way those values are spread — which values are common, which are rare, whether the data clusters symmetrically or leans to one side — is the distribution of the data. Reading the shape of a distribution is a core interpretation skill: it tells you whether the data is symmetric, skewed, or has unusual values at the extremes.

Symmetrical Distributions

A symmetrical distribution is balanced — the left and right sides are roughly mirror images of each other. In a perfectly symmetrical distribution, the mean, median, and mode are all equal and sit at the centre. A classic symmetrical shape is the bell curve, which you will encounter later in this lesson when looking at the Normal distribution.

Positive Skew

A positively skewed distribution has a longer tail on the right. Most values cluster at the lower end of the scale, with a few unusually high values stretching the tail to the right. Because those extreme high values pull the mean upwards, the mean is greater than the median in a positively skewed distribution.

A real-world example: household income in the UK is positively skewed. Most households earn in a moderate range, but a small number of very high earners stretch the tail. The mean income is pulled upwards by these high earners, making it higher than the median. This is why the median is often a more representative average for income data.

Negative Skew

A negatively skewed distribution has a longer tail on the left. Most values cluster at the higher end of the scale, with a few unusually low values stretching the tail to the left. The mean is pulled downwards by those extreme low values, making it less than the median.

A real-world example: scores on an easy test might show negative skew. Most students score highly (the cluster is on the right), but a small number of students who struggled pull the tail to the left. The mean score would be lower than the median because of those very low scores.

Key Fact

Positive skew: tail on the right, mean > median. Negative skew: tail on the left, mean < median. A useful memory trick: the skew is named after the direction of the TAIL, not the main cluster.

Key Fact

Positive skew: tail on the right, mean > median. Negative skew: tail on the left, mean < median. Symmetrical: mean = median. Remember: the skew is named after the direction of the TAIL, not where the main cluster sits.

Commenting on Outliers

An outlier is a value that stands apart from the rest of the data — either much larger or much smaller than typical. Outliers can arise from genuine extreme values (a student who scored 100% on a test where everyone else scored between 40% and 80%), measurement errors (a data entry typo turning 160 cm into 16 cm), or a genuinely different subgroup in the data.

When commenting on outliers in exam questions, you should: (1) identify the outlier by referring to its approximate value, (2) suggest whether it might be a genuine extreme value or a possible error, and (3) comment on its effect on any averages you have calculated. An outlier pulls the mean towards it but does not affect the median.

Students often say “positive skew has most values on the positive side of the graph.” This is wrong. Positive skew is named after the direction of the TAIL, not where the main cluster sits. In a positively skewed distribution, the TAIL goes right (in the positive direction) and the CLUSTER sits at the lower end.

A quick check: if someone earned the most money in a room, are they pulling the mean income up? Yes — so income data is likely positively skewed (long right tail, even though most people cluster at lower incomes). That is positive skew.

Binomial Distribution (Higher)

A binomial distribution describes the number of successes in a fixed number of independent trials, where each trial has the same probability of success. The word “binomial” will appear in your exam. The key characteristics are:

  • A fixed number of trials (e.g. flipping a coin 5 times).
  • Each trial has only two possible outcomes (success or failure).
  • The probability of success is constant across all trials.
  • The trials are independent of each other.

In your exam, the number of trials \(n\) will be no greater than 5. The distribution is symmetric when the probability of success is 0.5, and skewed when the probability is not 0.5. You do not need to use formal notation for the binomial distribution — describing its characteristics in words is sufficient.

The Normal Distribution and the 68/95 Rule (Higher)

The Normal distribution is a symmetric, bell-shaped distribution where values cluster around the mean and become progressively rarer further away. It describes many real-world characteristics: the heights of adults, birth weights, exam scores, and measurement errors all tend to follow approximately Normal distributions.

The specification requires you to know two key results about the Normal distribution:

  • Approximately 68% of the data lies within one standard deviation of the mean.
  • Approximately 95% of the data lies within two standard deviations of the mean.
  • Values more than three standard deviations from the mean are very unusual.

Action and Warning Lines in Quality Assurance (Higher)

In manufacturing and quality control, products are sampled regularly to check they meet a standard. The Normal distribution is used to set warning lines (at two standard deviations from the target) and action lines (at three standard deviations from the target). If a sample mean falls outside the action lines, the production process is stopped and investigated, because such a result would be very unusual if the process were running correctly.

Standardising Data (Higher)

To compare values from two different distributions (e.g. a student's score in Maths and their score in English, which have different means and standard deviations), you can standardise by converting each value to a z-score: $$z = rac{x - ar{x}}{s}$$ where \(x\) is the value, \( ar{x}\) is the mean, and \(s\) is the standard deviation. The formula will be given in the question. A z-score tells you how many standard deviations above or below the mean a value lies, allowing fair comparison across different scales.

The heights of a group of adults are Normally distributed with a mean of 170 cm and a standard deviation of 8 cm.

Within one standard deviation (162 cm to 178 cm): approximately 68% of adults. Within two standard deviations (154 cm to 186 cm): approximately 95% of adults. Heights above 194 cm or below 146 cm (three standard deviations away) are very unusual.
exam_tip_html: On questions asking you to describe or identify skew, always name the direction (“positive skew” or “negative skew”) AND describe the tail direction (“the tail stretches to the right”). For Higher questions about the Normal distribution and the 68/95 rule, show your working clearly: write out the calculation \( ext{mean} \pm 2 imes ext{standard deviation}\) before stating the range. On outlier questions, always comment on its effect on the mean compared to the median — this is frequently the second mark in a two-mark question.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Positive skew has a longer tail on the right (mean > median); negative skew has a longer tail on the left (mean < median); a symmetrical distribution has mean = median. The skew is named for the direction of the tail.
  • Outliers stand far apart from the main cluster, may be genuine extreme values or data errors, and pull the mean towards them without affecting the median.
  • Higher: the Normal distribution follows the 68/95 rule (68% within one standard deviation, 95% within two). Values more than three standard deviations from the mean are very unusual — this forms the basis of action and warning lines in quality control.

practice_questions.text:
The ages at which a group of people bought their first car are recorded. The distribution is positively skewed.
Which of the following statements about the mean and median is correct?
A) Mean < Median
B) Mean = Median
C) Mean > Median
D) The relationship between mean and median cannot be determined from skew alone.
practice_questions.marks: C [1 mark] — In a positively skewed distribution, the long right tail pulls the mean above the median.

practice_questions.text:
A dataset of 15 students' test scores is: 45, 48, 50, 51, 52, 53, 54, 55, 56, 58, 59, 60, 61, 62, 95.
The score of 95 appears to be an outlier.
Work out the mean and median of the dataset, and comment on the effect of the outlier on each.
practice_questions.marks:
Mean = (sum of all values) / 15. Sum = 45+48+50+51+52+53+54+55+56+58+59+60+61+62+95 = 859. Mean = 859/15 = 57.27 (accept 57.3) [1 mark].
Median = 8th value when ordered = 55 [1 mark].
Comment (for context): the outlier of 95 pulls the mean upwards (from approximately 55 to 57.3) but does not affect the median.

practice_questions.text:
A student looks at the following description of a distribution: 'Most values are clustered at the higher end of the scale, with a few very low values stretching the tail in the opposite direction.'
Describe the shape of this distribution, including the direction of the skew and the relative positions of the mean and median.
practice_questions.marks:
The distribution is negatively skewed [1].
The tail stretches to the left [1].
The mean is less than the median because the few low values pull the mean downwards [1].

practice_questions.text:
A production line fills packets of crisps with a target weight of 150 g. The weights are Normally distributed with a standard deviation of 4 g.
Calculate the range within which approximately 95% of packet weights will fall, and explain the significance of a packet weighing 162 g.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Calculation correct and explanation developed; Secure: Calculation correct with partial explanation.
95% range: mean +/- 2 standard deviations = 150 +/- 8 g = 142 g to 158 g [2 marks].
162 g is more than 3 standard deviations above the mean (150 + 3*4 = 162 g exactly) [1].
This is very unusual for a correctly running process and would trigger an investigation; it would fall outside the action line [1].

practice_questions.text:
A factory sets warning lines at two standard deviations from the target mean and action lines at three standard deviations. Samples are taken hourly.
Suggest and justify what the factory quality manager should do if three consecutive sample means fall between the warning line and the action line.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per suggestion and 1 mark per justification, up to 5 marks.
Mastering: A specific action and a justified reason linked to the statistical meaning of the warning/action lines.
- Monitor the process more closely or increase the sampling frequency [1] because three consecutive means between the warning and action lines suggests a trend away from the target, even though no individual result has crossed the action line [1].
- Investigate possible causes of drift (e.g. machine calibration, raw material variability) [1] before the means cross the action line and production needs to be stopped [1].
- Record and document the values so that patterns can be identified [1]; a sustained pattern of values above the warning line (even if none crosses the action line) is a known warning sign in quality control practice [1].
Secure: One specific action with a justified reason.
Developing: Names an action without justification.
Emerging: States 'do something' without specifying what.

practice_questions.text:
The scores in a maths test have a mean of 62 and a standard deviation of 12. The scores in an English test have a mean of 55 and a standard deviation of 8. A student scores 74 in maths and 71 in English.
Discuss in which subject the student performed better relative to their peers, using standardised scores in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks for a calculation, interpretation, comparison, and judgement.
Mastering: Both z-scores calculated correctly, interpreted, compared, and a judgement made.
- Maths z-score: (74 - 62) / 12 = 12/12 = 1.0 [1]. This means the maths score is 1 standard deviation above the mean [1].
- English z-score: (71 - 55) / 8 = 16/8 = 2.0 [1]. This means the English score is 2 standard deviations above the mean [1].
- Comparison: the student performed better relative to peers in English (z = 2.0) than in maths (z = 1.0), despite scoring lower in absolute terms [1].
- Judgement: the standardised score accounts for the different difficulty levels and spread of scores in each subject, making it a fairer comparison than comparing raw marks [1].
Secure: Both z-scores correct with interpretation.
Developing: One z-score calculated with partial interpretation.
Emerging: Compares raw scores only without standardising.

knowledge_checks.q: In a negatively skewed distribution, how do the mean and median compare?
options: It depends on the standard deviation

knowledge_checks.q: What percentage of data lies within two standard deviations of the mean in a Normal distribution?
A distribution with a longer tail on the right is called _____ skewed.
In quality control, the _____ lines are set at three standard deviations from the target mean and signal that the process must be stopped and investigated.

right: Mean is greater than the median
Mean is less than the median

flashcard_questions.q: In a positively skewed distribution, is the mean greater or less than the median?
flashcard_questions.a: Greater than the median; the long right tail pulls the mean upwards.

flashcard_questions.q: In a negatively skewed distribution, is the mean greater or less than the median?
flashcard_questions.a: Less than the median; the long left tail pulls the mean downwards.

flashcard_questions.q: Which direction does the tail go in a positively skewed distribution?

flashcard_questions.a: A data value that lies far from the main cluster of values in a dataset.

flashcard_questions.q: Does an outlier affect the mean or the median more?
flashcard_questions.a: The mean; outliers pull the mean towards them but do not affect the median.

flashcard_questions.q: What percentage of data lies within one standard deviation of the mean in a Normal distribution? (Higher)
What percentage of data lies within two standard deviations of the mean in a Normal distribution? (Higher)
What are the four characteristics of a binomial distribution? (Higher)
flashcard_questions.a: Fixed number of trials; two outcomes; constant probability of success; independent trials.

flashcard_questions.q: At what distance from the mean do action lines sit in quality control? (Higher)
flashcard_questions.a: Three standard deviations from the target mean.

flashcard_questions.q: What does standardising data allow you to do? (Higher)
flashcard_questions.a: Compare values from distributions with different means and standard deviations on a common scale.

glossary_terms.definition: The pattern of how values in a dataset are spread, showing which values occur frequently and which occur rarely.
A distribution where the left and right sides are roughly mirror images of each other, with the mean, median and mode all at the centre.
A distribution with a longer tail on the right-hand side, where most values are clustered at the lower end and a few high values pull the mean above the median.
A distribution with a longer tail on the left-hand side, where most values are clustered at the higher end and a few low values pull the mean below the median.
A data value that lies far away from the main cluster of values in a dataset.
A probability distribution that arises when counting the number of successes in a fixed number of independent trials, each with the same probability of success.
A symmetric, bell-shaped probability distribution where most values cluster near the mean and become increasingly rare further from the mean.
Lines on a quality control chart set at two standard deviations from the target mean; a value outside these lines suggests the process may need monitoring.
Lines on a quality control chart set at three standard deviations from the target mean; a value outside these lines indicates the process should be stopped and investigated.
